insight: 경쟁자가 몇 안 되는 시장에서 내 가격은 고객에게 하는 제안이 아니라 경쟁사가 즉시 대응하는 '수'다. 그래서 경쟁은 가격보다 따라 하기 어려운 것으로 옮겨 간다.

cards.title: Why four firms audit almost every giant company
body: If you run one of the world's largest listed companies and need an auditor, your real shortlist is four names: Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG.
There used to be eight. How a market shrinks to four, and how those four behave, explains a lot about pricing in any business with few rivals.

image.label: Four tall office towers standing apart from a crowd of small buildings
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 건물들이 빽빽한 도시 위로 비슷한 높이의 고층 빌딩 네 채가 우뚝 서 있음. 빌딩에는 실제 회사 로고나 이름을 쓰지 않고 단색으로만 구분.

cards.title: Should you cut your price to win contracts?
body: You run one of three industrial laundry firms that serve hospitals in your region. Contracts are rebid every year, and all three firms see who won what.
You could cut your price 10% to win two big hospitals from rivals. What do you do?

options.text: Cut 10% across the board and grab share
options.feedback: You may win this round, but your two rivals will see it and match at the next bid. Then all three earn 10% less and nobody has more share.

options.text: Hold your price and compete on reliability and turnaround time
options.feedback: You give up a quick win, but you avoid a cut rivals can copy in a week. Service is slower to copy than a price.

options.text: Cut the price only for the two hospitals you want
options.feedback: Narrower risk, but with three firms and public rebids, rivals will learn and respond. You've likely just lowered the price for those contracts for good.

cards.title: From eight firms to four.
body: In the 1980s, the largest accounting firms were called the Big Eight. Mergers cut them to six, then five when Price Waterhouse and Coopers & Lybrand joined to form PwC in 1998.
In 2002, Arthur Andersen collapsed after the Enron scandal. That left four.

Big companies need auditors with offices worldwide and deep industry teams. Few firms can offer that, so the field stayed small. In 2019, the UK's competition regulator studied the market and proposed reforms, worried that big companies had too little choice.

image.label: Timeline of eight circles merging into four
image.brief: 타임라인 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 원 8개 → 6개 → 5개 → 4개로 합쳐지는 흐름. 1998 표시에 두 원이 합쳐지고, 2002 표시에 원 하나가 사라짐. 실제 로고 없이 색깔 원만 사용.

cards.title: Oligopoly
body: An **oligopoly** is a market with only a few large sellers, each big enough that its moves change the results of the others.

The key word is *interdependence*. In a crowded market, one seller's price cut goes unnoticed. In an oligopoly, every rival notices and reacts. So each decision is less like setting a price and more like making a move in a game.

cards.title: Why price cuts rarely win.
body: When rivals are few, the pattern is predictable:
list: **Moves are visible:** rivals see your price within days
**Cuts get matched:** nobody wants to lose share, so the cut spreads
**Everyone earns less:** shares end up roughly where they started
**Competition shifts:** firms compete on reputation, expertise and service instead
cards.callout: Audit firms are a good example: clients often choose on industry expertise and trust, not on the lowest fee.
cards.softwareNote: Cloud infrastructure is run by a handful of large providers. They rarely win by headline price cuts alone, and compete hard on features, tools and the cost of switching away.

cards.title: Oligopolies are often local.
body: You don't need a global industry to be in one. A town with three hardware stores, a city with two concrete suppliers, or a region with three hospital laundries are all oligopolies.

The number that matters is not how many firms exist in your country. It's how many your customer realistically compares. If that number is small, your rivals will react to you, and you should plan for it.

cards.title: Watching rivals is fine. Agreeing with them isn't.
body: Reacting to a rival's public price is normal competition. Talking with rivals about prices, bids or who serves which customer is price fixing, which is illegal in most countries.
Oligopolies also don't last forever. New entrants, big buyers who push back, or regulators who step in can all change the game. A comfortable market of three can become a crowded market quickly.

cards.title: Now it's a food distributor.
body: You're one of three wholesalers delivering to restaurants in your city. One rival just cut prices 5% on staples like oil, flour and rice. A few chefs have asked if you'll match.

options.text: Match 5% on everything you sell, right away
options.feedback: You protect share, but you cut margin on products nobody compared. The third rival will likely follow, and all three earn less.

options.text: Call the rival's owner and suggest you both go back to old prices
options.feedback: It might feel like a sensible truce, but it's price fixing. The legal risk is far larger than any margin you'd save.

options.text: Match only on the few staples chefs compare, and push your delivery reliability
options.feedback: You remove the reason to switch without cutting every price. Then you compete on what's harder to copy than a price tag.

cards.title: With few rivals, every price is a move they'll answer.
body: Before changing a price, ask what your rivals will do next, and where you'd stand after they do it. Then compete on what they can't copy in a week.
**Try it today:** list the rivals your customers actually compare you with. For each, write down how fast they would match a 10% price cut.
